claims.source: Rsp consists of a dimer of two closely related ~120 bp repeats in the pericentric heterochromatin on chromosome 2R of D. melanogaster (Wu et al., 1988; Pimpinelli and Dimitri, 1989).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: The 1.688 family of repeats is the most abundant complex satDNA in D. melanogaster.
claims.source: The 1.688 family of repeats is the most abundant complex satDNA in D. melanogaster (Lohe and Roberts, 1988).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: The 1.688 family comprises different subfamilies that exist as discrete tandem arrays in the pericentric heterochromatin on chromosomes 2L, 3L, and X.
claims.source: It comprises different subfamilies that exist as discrete tandem arrays in the pericentric heterochromatin named after their repeat unit sizes on chromosome 2L (260-bp), chromosome 3L (353-bp and 356-bp), and the X chromosome (359-bp) (Losada and Villasante, 1996; Abad et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Both Rsp and 1.688 satDNA families are expressed in gonads, head, and other tissues.
claims.source: Both satDNA families are expressed in gonads, head, and other tissues (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by analysis of modENCODE RNA-seq datasets shown in figures.

claims.claim: Rsp and 1.688 transcript abundance is low (RPMRsp < 10 and RPM1.688 < 300).
claims.source: Their transcript abundance is low (RPMRsp < 10 and RPM1.688 < 300; Supplementary file 2) and generally increases throughout development and with adult age (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by quantification of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: SatDNA transcript abundance generally increases throughout development and with adult age.
claims.source: Their transcript abundance is low (RPMRsp < 10 and RPM1.688 < 300; Supplementary file 2) and generally increases throughout development and with adult age (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by analysis of modENCODE RNA-seq datasets across developmental stages.

claims.claim: The majority of satDNA transcripts are not polyadenylated.
claims.source: SatDNA-derived reads have very low abundance in the poly-A selected RNA-seq data (RPMRsp < 0.2 and RPM1.688 < 10; Supplementary file 2), indicating that the majority of satDNA transcripts are not polyadenylated.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the low abundance of satDNA reads in poly-A selected RNA-seq compared to total RNA-seq.

claims.claim: Both Rsp and 1.688 satellite transcripts are visible in testes and ovaries by RNA FISH.
claims.source: Both Rsp and 1.688 satellite transcripts are visible in testes and ovaries (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by RNA FISH experiments shown in the figures.

claims.claim: SatDNA FISH signals are from RNA rather than DNA.
claims.source: These signals are undetectable after treating with RNaseA prior to probe hybridization (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), which degrades single-stranded RNAs, or RNaseH post-probe hybridization (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), which degrades the RNA in DNA-RNA hybrids. This suggests that these signals are from RNA rather than DNA.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNase treatment controls in RNA FISH experiments.

claims.claim: SatDNA transcript foci are detected in ovarian nurse cells and in pre-meiotic testicular germ cells.
claims.source: We detected satDNA transcript foci in ovarian nurse cells and in pre-meiotic testicular germ cells.
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by RNA FISH imaging data.

claims.claim: In testes, Rsp signal is detected at earlier stages of spermatogenesis than 1.688 signals.
claims.source: Interestingly, in testes we detected Rsp signal at earlier stages of spermatogenesis (i.e., germline stem cells/spermatogonia) than the 1.688 signals (i.e., primary spermatocytes; Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by RNA FISH imaging showing differential timing of expression.

claims.claim: Rsp is the specific target of Segregation Distorter (SD), a male meiotic drive system.
claims.source: The difference in timing is notable as Rsp is the specific target of Segregation Distorter (SD; Sandler et al., 1959): a well-known male meiotic drive system that causes a defect in post-meiotic germ cells (reviewed in Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Rsp transcript abundance correlates with its genomic copy number.
claims.source: Signal quantification (shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) shows Rsp transcript abundance correlates with its genomic copy number (Pearson's correlation coefficient r2 = 0.93, p-value=0.02).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by northern blot quantification and qPCR/qRT-PCR data.

claims.claim: Rsp transcript lengths range between <300 nt and >9000 nt.
claims.source: We determined that, while transcript lengths were similar among these lines—ranging between <300 nt and >9000 nt (Figure 1C)—the abundance of Rsp transcripts correlated with genomic copy number (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 4, Pearson's correlation coefficient r2 = 0.93, p-value=0.02).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by northern blot analysis showing transcript size distribution.

claims.claim: The correlation between genomic copy number and transcript abundance is consistent with most transcripts originating from the large blocks of heterochromatic satDNA.
claims.source: The correlation between genomic copy number and transcript abundance is consistent with most transcripts originating from the large blocks of heterochromatic satDNA.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between copy number and expression level.

claims.claim: The majority of satDNA-derived small RNAs are piRNAs.
claims.source: Our results suggest that the majority of these satDNA-derived small RNAs are piRNAs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of evidence including size distribution, ping-pong signatures, and PIWI protein binding.

claims.claim: An average of 90% of satDNA-derived small RNAs range from 23 nt to 28 nt, with a peak at 24–26 nt.
claims.source: First, these small RNAs are abundant in testes and ovaries, and their size distribution is typical for piRNA populations: an average of 90% of the RNAs range from 23 nt to 28 nt, with a peak at 24–26 nt in D. melanogaster (Brennecke et al., 2007; Figure 2A for Rsp and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C for 1.688).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by small RNA-seq size distribution analysis.

claims.claim: SatDNA-derived small RNAs bear a signature of the piRNA-guided RNA cleavage process called the ping-pong cycle.
claims.source: Second, the satDNA-derived small RNAs bear a signature of the piRNA-guided RNA cleavage process called the ping-pong cycle.
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by analysis showing 10 nt overlap of antisense-sense piRNAs with 1U/10A bias.

claims.claim: SatDNA-derived small RNAs have a ping-pong signature with Z-score = 4.55 for Rsp and 6.85 for 1.688 satellite.
claims.source: Our analysis of the ovary small RNA-seq data (Mohn et al., 2014; Andersen et al., 2017; Parhad et al., 2017) confirms a ping-pong signature for satDNA-derived small RNAs: Z-score = 4.55 for Rsp and 6.85 for 1.688 satellite (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, G) and ~60–80% have 1U/10A (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, F).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by computational analysis of small RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: ~60–80% of satDNA-derived small RNAs have 1U/10A nucleotide bias.
claims.source: Our analysis of the ovary small RNA-seq data (Mohn et al., 2014; Andersen et al., 2017; Parhad et al., 2017) confirms a ping-pong signature for satDNA-derived small RNAs: Z-score = 4.55 for Rsp and 6.85 for 1.688 satellite (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, G) and ~60–80% have 1U/10A (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, F).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by computational analysis of small RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: SatDNA-derived small RNAs are bound by the PIWI proteins Piwi, Aubergine, and Argonaute3.
claims.source: Third, satDNA-derived small RNAs are bound by the PIWI proteins, as expected for piRNAs. Our reanalysis of published Piwi, Aubergine (Aub), and Argonaute3 (Ago3) RIP-seq data from ovaries (Brennecke et al., 2007; Mohn et al., 2015; Sato et al., 2015) shows that Rsp and 1.688 RNAs interact with each of these proteins (Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by reanalysis of published RIP-seq data.

claims.claim: ~0.9% and 0.1% of Piwi-bound RNAs map to 1.688 and Rsp, respectively.
claims.source: For example, ~0.9% and 0.1% of Piwi-bound RNAs map to 1.688 and Rsp, respectively.
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by quantification of RIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Only an average of 0.0005% of the reads from Piwi RIP-seq data mapped to miRNAs.
claims.source: In contrast, only an average of 0.0005% of the reads from Piwi RIP-seq data mapped to miRNAs, which are abundant small RNAs not known to be bound by Piwi.
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by quantification of RIP-seq data and serves as a negative control.

claims.claim: The distribution of piRNA read depth is not uniform along the length of single monomers or dimers of satDNA repeats.
claims.source: We find that the distribution of piRNA read depth is not uniform along the length of single monomers (359-bp and 260-bp) or dimers (Rsp) of these satDNA repeats (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by analysis of piRNA read pileup along consensus sequences.

claims.claim: The piRNA read pileup pattern differs between ovaries and testes.
claims.source: The piRNA read pileup pattern also differs between ovaries and testes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B), suggesting that there may be differences in transcription machinery, precursor production, or precursor processing between these tissues.
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by comparison of piRNA read pileup patterns between tissues.

claims.claim: SatDNAs are transcribed from both strands.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that satDNAs are transcribed from both strands, similar to dual-strand piRNA clusters.
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by RNA-seq read mapping showing nearly 1:1 ratio of plus and minus strand reads.

claims.claim: For all genomic copies of Rsp or 1.688 satDNA, there is a nearly 1:1 ratio of reads mapping to the plus and minus strands.
claims.source: Collectively, for all genomic copies of Rsp or 1.688 satDNA (all subfamilies), we find a nearly 1:1 ratio of reads mapping to the plus and minus strands (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A; all mapped and uniquely mapped reads).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by RNA-seq read mapping analysis.

claims.claim: Dual-strand piRNA clusters are associated with the heterochromatin binding protein Rhino.
claims.source: Dual-strand piRNA clusters are associated with the heterochromatin binding protein Rhi (Klattenhoff et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Dual-strand piRNA clusters have higher Rhino enrichment (mean enrichment ChIP/Input Edual = 9.08) compared to uni-strand piRNA clusters (Euni = 1.69).
claims.source: Our results for piRNA clusters are consistent with previous studies (Klattenhoff et al., 2009; Mohn et al., 2014; Andersen et al., 2017): the dual-strand piRNA clusters have higher Rhi enrichment (mean enrichment ChIP/Input Edual = 9.08) compared to uni-strand piRNA clusters (Euni = 1.69; pairwise t-test with Benjamini–Hochberg; Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995 adjusted p-value Padj=0.01) and euchromatic genes (Eeuch = 1.55; Padj=0.01).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by reanalysis of published Rhino ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Complex satDNAs are in the top 30% of all repeats enriched in Rhino.
claims.source: We found that complex satDNAs are in the top 30% of all repeats enriched in Rhi (full data in Figure 2—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by analysis of Rhino ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: The level of Rhino enrichment for satDNAs (Esat = 4.70) is intermediate between dual-strand piRNA clusters and uni-strand piRNA clusters or euchromatin.
claims.source: The level of Rhi enrichment for satDNAs (Esat = 4.70) is intermediate between the highly enriched dual-strand piRNA clusters (Padj=0.1) and the minimally Rhi enriched uni-strand piRNA clusters (Padj=0.01) or euchromatin (Padj=0.01 Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by quantification and statistical analysis of Rhino ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: The distribution of Rhino ChIP-seq reads is similar to the alignment depth of genomic repeats.
claims.source: Unlike the uneven distribution of piRNAs along satellite monomers/dimers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B), the distribution of Rhi ChIP-seq reads (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D) is similar to the alignment depth of genomic repeats (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by comparison of ChIP-seq read distribution with genomic repeat distribution.

claims.claim: Rhino localizes to the large satDNA genomic loci rather than a subset of smaller clusters or repeats across the genome.
claims.source: This suggests that Rhi localizes to the large satDNA genomic loci rather than a subset of smaller clusters or repeats across the genome (e.g., the 12 copies of Rsp inside an intron of Ago3 on chromosome 3L; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) or in potentially unannotated piRNA clusters.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the uniform distribution of Rhino ChIP-seq reads across satDNA loci.

claims.claim: In rhi mutants, Rsp piRNA abundance is 0.2–6.3% their levels in wild-type datasets.
claims.source: In rhi mutants, Rsp piRNA abundance is 0.2–6.3% their levels in wild-type datasets.
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by quantification of small RNA-seq data from rhi mutants.

claims.claim: In rhi mutants, piRNA abundance for 1.688 is 1.4–7.8% their levels in wild-type datasets.
claims.source: Similarly, piRNA abundance for 1.688 is 1.4–7.8% their levels in wild-type datasets (complete list of log2 fold change for satDNAs in Supplementary files 6 and 7).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by quantification of small RNA-seq data from rhi mutants.

claims.claim: The reduction in satDNA piRNA level is robust to normalization method.
claims.source: The reduction in satDNA piRNA level is robust to normalization method (miRNA in Figure 3A; flamenco cluster in Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by analysis using different normalization approaches.

claims.claim: piRNA production from complex satDNAs is regulated by the heterochromatin-dependent transcription machinery associated with dual-strand piRNA clusters.
claims.source: Overall, our results indicate that piRNA production from complex satDNAs is regulated by the heterochromatin-dependent transcription machinery associated with dual-strand piRNA clusters.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the finding that satDNA piRNA levels are reduced in RDC and Moon mutants.

claims.claim: RDC and Moon mutants affect piRNA precursor transcription at the dual-strand piRNA clusters 42AB and 80F.
claims.source: RDC and Moon mutants affect piRNA precursor transcription at the dual-strand piRNA clusters 42AB and 80F (Mohn et al., 2014; Andersen et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Decreases in steady-state long RNA transcript levels were detected at dual-strand piRNA clusters in RDC and Moon mutants.
claims.source: Consistent with published reports, we detected decreases in steady-state long RNA transcript levels at dual-strand piRNA clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by reanalysis of total RNA-seq data from mutants.

claims.claim: No significant decrease in steady-state long RNA transcript levels for satDNAs was observed in RDC and Moon mutants.
claims.source: However, we did not observe a significant decrease in steady-state long RNA transcript levels for satDNAs (Supplementary file 8).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by analysis of total RNA-seq data from mutants.

claims.claim: Rsp expression level is lower, but not significantly so, in rhi and moon mutants compared to wild type (p-value=0.048 and 0.077).
claims.source: After controlling for genomic repeat copy number with qPCR (Figure 3B), Rsp expression level is lower, but not significantly so in rhi and moon mutants compared to wild type (p-value=0.048 and 0.077; Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by qRT-PCR experiments.

claims.claim: The abundance of poly-A transcripts is increased for Rsp and unchanged for 1.688 in rhi mutant relative to wild type.
claims.source: However, when we reanalyzed the total and poly-A selected RNA-seq data from the rhi mutant (ElMaghraby et al., 2019), we find that the abundance of poly-A transcripts (which are likely a subset of non-precursors) is increased for Rsp and unchanged for 1.688 (Supplementary file 9) relative to wild type.
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by reanalysis of published RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Changes in piRNA precursor levels may be masked by the non-precursor levels in rhi mutants.
claims.source: This result suggests that changes in piRNA precursor levels may be masked by the non-precursor levels, similar to reports on piRNA cluster transcription in embryonic piwi knockdown ovaries (Akkouche et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that poly-A transcripts increase while total transcripts do not significantly decrease.

claims.claim: piRNA production for all complex satDNA is regulated by the primary piRNA pathway (Gasz, Vreteno, Shutdown), UAP56, and the ping-pong pathway (Ago3, Krimper).
claims.source: Our reanalysis of these data suggests that piRNA production for all complex satDNA is regulated by the primary piRNA pathway (Gasz, Vreteno, Shutdown), UAP56, and the ping-pong pathway (Ago3, Krimper).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by reanalysis of small RNA-seq data from multiple mutants.

claims.claim: piRNA production at satDNA loci is regulated by the dual-strand piRNA pathway.
claims.source: While further work is required to determine all of the components involved in processing satDNA transcripts, our results suggest that piRNA production at satDNA loci is regulated by the dual-strand piRNA pathway.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on analysis of multiple mutants in the piRNA pathway.

claims.claim: SatDNAs are enriched for H3K9me3 in ovaries.
claims.source: Consistent with their Rhi enrichment, we find that satDNAs are enriched for H3K9me3 in ovaries (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B; datasets from Klenov et al., 2014; Le Thomas et al., 2014; Mohn et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by reanalysis of published H3K9me3 ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Piwi plays an important role in establishing H3K9 methylation on euchromatic TEs in ovaries.
claims.source: Piwi plays an important role in establishing H3K9 methylation on euchromatic TEs in ovaries (Mohn et al., 2014) and heterochromatin more generally in embryos (Akkouche et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Transiently knocking down piwi expression early in the embryonic germline leads to a general decrease in H3K9me3 in the adult ovary.
claims.source: Transiently knocking down piwi expression early in the embryonic germline leads to a general decrease in H3K9me3 in the adult ovary, and a specific decrease in piRNA production and increase in spliced non-precursor transcripts at dual-strand piRNA clusters (Akkouche et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: A decrease of H3K9me3 at satDNAs was detected in embryonic piwi knock down ovaries.
claims.source: We therefore reanalyzed H3K9me3 ChIP-seq data from embryonic piwi knock down ovaries (Akkouche et al., 2017). We detected a decrease of H3K9me3 at satDNAs (Figure 4A), suggesting that Piwi is also required for the establishment of heterochromatin at these loci.
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by reanalysis of published H3K9me3 ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Piwi is required for the establishment of heterochromatin at satDNA loci.
claims.source: We detected a decrease of H3K9me3 at satDNAs (Figure 4A), suggesting that Piwi is also required for the establishment of heterochromatin at these loci.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the decrease in H3K9me3 at satDNAs in piwi knockdown.

claims.claim: piRNA production from satDNAs is reduced in embryonic piwi knockdown.
claims.source: Consistent with the decrease in H3K9me3, piRNA production from satDNAs is also reduced (with some variation among replicates observed for Rsp; Figure 4B); and satDNA total RNA levels are increased (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), similar to dual-strand piRNA clusters (Akkouche et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by reanalysis of small RNA-seq data from piwi knockdown.

claims.claim: satDNA total RNA levels are increased in embryonic piwi knockdown.
claims.source: Consistent with the decrease in H3K9me3, piRNA production from satDNAs is also reduced (with some variation among replicates observed for Rsp; Figure 4B); and satDNA total RNA levels are increased (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), similar to dual-strand piRNA clusters (Akkouche et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by reanalysis of total RNA-seq data from piwi knockdown.

claims.claim: Piwi is important for heterochromatin establishment at piRNA clusters but appears to be dispensable for heterochromatin maintenance.
claims.source: While Piwi is important for heterochromatin establishment at piRNA clusters, it appears to be dispensable for heterochromatin maintenance (Czech et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: Depleting Piwi in the nucleus affects H3K9me3 level on a subset of active transposons, but not on piRNA clusters.
claims.source: Depleting Piwi in the nucleus with piwi mutants lacking a nuclear localization signal (NLS; Klenov et al., 2014), or knocking down germline piwi (Le Thomas et al., 2013; Mohn et al., 2014) affects H3K9me3 level on a subset of active transposons, but not on piRNA clusters (Klenov et al., 2014; Mohn et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: The level of H3K9me3 on satDNAs is largely unchanged in piwi knockdown or mutant ovaries.
claims.source: Similar to piRNA clusters, our reanalysis of these data shows that the level of H3K9me3 on satDNAs is largely unchanged in the knockdown or mutant ovaries (with some variation observed among datasets; Supplementary file 10).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by reanalysis of H3K9me3 ChIP-seq data from piwi mutants/knockdowns.

claims.claim: Piwi plays a role in establishing, but not maintaining, heterochromatin at satDNAs in early embryos.
claims.source: These analyses suggest a role for Piwi in establishing, but not maintaining, heterochromatin at satDNAs in early embryos, which is important for producing piRNAs later in adult ovaries.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the differential effects of embryonic vs. adult piwi depletion on H3K9me3 at satDNAs.

claims.claim: Complex satDNA transcription is regulated in a manner similar to dual-strand piRNA clusters in the female germline.
claims.source: Here we show that transcription from satDNAs is regulated by the heterochromatin-dependent RDC machinery and Moon in ovaries and these transcripts are processed into piRNAs. Thus, complex satDNA transcription is regulated in a manner similar to dual-strand piRNA clusters in the female germline (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple lines of evidence showing satDNAs share characteristics with dual-strand piRNA clusters.

claims.claim: The findings are consistent with a study that detected bidirectional transcription of the 1.688 satDNA family in ovaries.
claims.source: Our findings are consistent with a study that detected bidirectional transcription of the 1.688 satDNA family in ovaries (Usakin et al., 2007) and a recent analysis of satDNA-derived piRNAs in RDC mutants (Chen et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement relates the current findings to previous published work.

claims.claim: 1.688 transcript abundance is elevated in mutants of two piRNA processing genes, spn-E and aub.
claims.source: Usakin et al. found that 1.688 transcript abundance is elevated in mutants of two piRNA processing genes, spn-E and aub (Usakin et al., 2007), suggesting that 1.688 is targeted by piRNAs, similar to TEs.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: Most satellite-derived transcripts and small RNAs come from the heterochromatin-dependent transcription of the large satDNA blocks.
claims.source: Here we provide evidence that most satellite-derived transcripts and small RNAs reported in previous studies (Aravin et al., 2003; Saito et al., 2006; Usakin et al., 2007; Rošić et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021) come from the heterochromatin-dependent transcription of the large satDNA blocks.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the correlation between copy number and expression, and the dependence on RDC machinery.

claims.claim: Proportionally, far fewer piRNAs in the male germline are derived from TEs than in the female germline.
claims.source: Proportionally, far fewer piRNAs in the male germline are derived from TEs than in the female germline (Nishida et al., 2007; Nagao et al., 2010; Quénerch'du et al., 2016), suggesting roles outside of TE repression.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Recent studies implicate piRNA pathways in intragenomic conflicts such as male meiotic drive.
claims.source: For example, recent studies implicate piRNA pathways in intragenomic conflicts (e.g., male meiotic drive; Gell and Reenan, 2013; Courret et al., 2019), with satDNAs often at the center of these conflicts.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Maternal deposition of Piwi contributes to heterochromatin establishment in the embryo.
claims.source: Maternal deposition of Piwi contributes to heterochromatin establishment in the embryo (Gu and Elgin, 2013), and Piwi-dependent H3K9me3 deposition at canonical piRNA clusters is important for subsequent piRNA production at piRNA clusters (Akkouche et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Piwi-dependent H3K9me3 deposition at canonical piRNA clusters is important for subsequent piRNA production at piRNA clusters.
claims.source: Maternal deposition of Piwi contributes to heterochromatin establishment in the embryo (Gu and Elgin, 2013), and Piwi-dependent H3K9me3 deposition at canonical piRNA clusters is important for subsequent piRNA production at piRNA clusters (Akkouche et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: Both H3K9me3 chromatin and piRNA production from complex satDNA is reduced when transiently depleting Piwi in the embryos.
claims.source: Similar to piRNA clusters, we found evidence that both H3K9me3 chromatin and piRNA production from complex satDNA is reduced when transiently depleting Piwi in the embryos, suggesting a role for the piRNA pathway in heterochromatin establishment at satDNA loci (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by reanalysis of ChIP-seq and small RNA-seq data from embryonic piwi knockdown.

claims.claim: Piwi, guided by satDNA-derived piRNAs, establishes H3K9me3 at satDNA, marking the satDNAs as piRNA production sites later in development.
claims.source: We propose a simple model of self-regulation, where Piwi, guided by satDNA-derived piRNAs, establishes H3K9me3 at satDNA, marking the satDNAs as piRNA production sites later in development (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data showing Piwi-dependent heterochromatin establishment and piRNA production at satDNAs.

claims.claim: Piwi might not be the only factor necessary for heterochromatin establishment in embryos.
claims.source: While a contributor, Piwi might not be the only factor necessary for heterochromatin establishment in embryos (Wei et al., 2021a).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: Once established, the maintenance of heterochromatin at piRNA clusters and satDNAs is not Piwi-dependent.
claims.source: And once established, the maintenance of heterochromatin at piRNA clusters and satDNAs is not Piwi-dependent (Supplementary file 10; Klenov et al., 2014; Mohn et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data analysis and citations to published studies.

claims.claim: The piRNA pathway is likely to be one of several factors important for proper packaging and regulation of repeat-rich regions of the genome.
claims.source: Therefore, the piRNA pathway is likely to be one of several factors important for proper packaging and regulation of repeat-rich regions of the genome (Pal-Bhadra et al., 2004; Gu and Elgin, 2013).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the data and supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Heterochromatic regions form a distinct phase-separated nuclear compartment that contributes to nuclear organization and gene regulation.
claims.source: First, heterochromatic regions form a distinct phase-separated nuclear compartment that contributes to nuclear organization and gene regulation (Larson et al., 2017; Strom et al., 2017), and chromocenter formation (Jagannathan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Unregulated satDNA may disrupt nuclear organization and lead to cell death.
claims.source: Unregulated satDNA may disrupt this organization (Novo et al., 2020) and lead to cell death (Jagannathan et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: De-repressed satDNA may lead to genome instability including chromosomal structural rearrangements.
claims.source: Second, de-repressed satDNA may lead to genome instability (Peng and Karpen, 2007) including chromosomal structural rearrangements (reviewed in Janssen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies and reviews.

claims.claim: Rearrangements involving satDNA may lead to mitotic defects in the developing embryo as they can affect chromosome segregation.
claims.source: In the short term, rearrangements involving satDNA may lead to mitotic defects in the developing embryo as they can affect chromosome segregation (Ferree and Barbash, 2009; Ferree, 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Over longer evolutionary time scales, rearrangements contribute to variation in satDNA organization between individuals and species, and may cause genetic incompatibilities between closely related species.
claims.source: Over longer evolutionary time scales, these rearrangements contribute to variation in satDNA organization between individuals and species, and may cause genetic incompatibilities between closely related species (Ferree and Barbash, 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: SatDNAs are among the most rapidly evolving sequences in genomes.
claims.source: SatDNAs are indeed among the most rapidly evolving sequences in genomes (reviewed in Ferree and Prasad, 2012; Plohl et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claims.claim: The piRNA pathway regulates satDNA.
claims.source: Our finding that the piRNA pathway regulates satDNA suggests a general role for the piRNA pathway and for maternal satDNA-derived RNAs in remodeling chromatin in the developing embryo.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the findings presented in the study.

claims.claim: The piRNA pathway has a general role in remodeling chromatin in the developing embryo.
claims.source: Our finding that the piRNA pathway regulates satDNA suggests a general role for the piRNA pathway and for maternal satDNA-derived RNAs in remodeling chromatin in the developing embryo.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the finding that satDNA-derived piRNAs contribute to heterochromatin establishment.

claims.claim: Initial establishment of heterochromatin may be an important step in ensuring genome integrity throughout development and in adult tissues.
claims.source: This initial establishment of heterochromatin may be an important step in ensuring genome integrity throughout development and in adult tissues, but this remains an open question.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential importance of heterochromatin establishment.

results.result: Complex satDNAs (Rsp and 1.688) are transcribed into long noncoding RNAs in Drosophila germline tissues. These transcripts are detected in ovaries and testes by RNA-seq and RNA FISH, are predominantly non-polyadenylated, and their abundance correlates with genomic copy number, indicating transcription from large heterochromatic satDNA blocks.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C32-C43 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (RNA-seq, RNA FISH, northern blot, qRT-PCR) demonstrating satDNA transcription. The correlation between copy number and expression (C41, r²=0.93, p=0.02) and RNase controls (C37) strengthen the conclusion. The data consistently support transcription from heterochromatic loci.

results.result: SatDNA-derived transcripts are processed into piRNAs in the Drosophila germline. These small RNAs exhibit characteristic piRNA features: 23-28 nt size distribution peaking at 24-26 nt, ping-pong signatures (Z-scores 4.55 for Rsp, 6.85 for 1.688), 1U/10A nucleotide bias (60-80%), and binding to PIWI proteins (Piwi, Aub, Ago3).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C44-C51 provide multiple independent lines of evidence (size distribution, ping-pong analysis, nucleotide bias, RIP-seq) that collectively demonstrate satDNA-derived small RNAs are bona fide piRNAs. The miRNA negative control (C51) and quantitative RIP-seq data (C50) strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: SatDNAs are transcribed bidirectionally from both DNA strands, similar to dual-strand piRNA clusters. RNA-seq analysis shows a nearly 1:1 ratio of reads mapping to plus and minus strands for both all mapped and uniquely mapped reads.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are supported by strand-specific RNA-seq data showing balanced bidirectional transcription. The analysis includes both all mapped reads and uniquely mapped reads to assembled satDNA loci, providing robust evidence for dual-strand transcription.

results.result: SatDNA piRNA production depends on the Rhino-Deadlock-Cutoff (RDC) complex and Moonshiner. SatDNAs show intermediate Rhino enrichment (Esat=4.70) between dual-strand piRNA clusters and euchromatin. In RDC and Moon mutants, satDNA piRNA levels are dramatically reduced (0.2-7.8% of wild-type levels), indicating dependence on heterochromatin-dependent transcription machinery.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C56-C65 provide strong evidence through ChIP-seq showing Rhino enrichment at satDNAs and small RNA-seq from multiple mutant datasets showing consistent reduction in satDNA piRNAs. The results are robust to normalization method (C64) and consistent across multiple independent studies.

results.result: RDC and Moon mutants affect steady-state transcript levels differently at piRNA clusters versus satDNAs. While dual-strand piRNA cluster transcripts decrease significantly in mutants, satDNA total RNA levels show no significant decrease, though qRT-PCR shows marginally non-significant decreases (p=0.048, 0.077). Poly-A transcript analysis suggests piRNA precursor changes may be masked by non-precursor transcripts.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C71 reveal a discrepancy between piRNA reduction and total RNA levels at satDNAs. While C67 shows expected decreases at piRNA clusters, C68-C69 show no significant changes at satDNAs. The interpretation (C71) that precursor changes are masked is speculative and requires additional experiments to distinguish precursor from non-precursor transcripts. The p-values (0.048, 0.077) are borderline and would not survive multiple testing correction.

results.result: SatDNA piRNA production is regulated by components of the primary piRNA pathway (Gasz, Vreteno, Shutdown), UAP56, and the ping-pong pathway (Ago3, Krimper), suggesting regulation by the dual-strand piRNA pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are based on reanalysis of multiple datasets, but the authors acknowledge variability between datasets for some mutants (e.g., Zucchini shows opposite effects in different studies). While consistent patterns emerge for some factors, the inconsistencies and lack of validation experiments make this conclusion uncertain. Further work is explicitly stated as required (C73).

results.result: The piRNA pathway, specifically Piwi, is important for establishing heterochromatin at satDNAs in early embryos. Embryonic piwi knockdown leads to decreased H3K9me3 at satDNAs, reduced satDNA piRNA production, and increased total satDNA RNA levels, similar to effects at dual-strand piRNA clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C74-C80, C93 provide consistent evidence from reanalysis of published ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing that embryonic Piwi depletion affects both H3K9me3 levels and piRNA production at satDNAs. The parallel with piRNA clusters (C76, C80) strengthens the interpretation. However, all data are from reanalysis of published datasets rather than new experiments.

results.result: Piwi is required for heterochromatin establishment but not maintenance at satDNAs. Embryonic Piwi depletion reduces H3K9me3 at satDNAs, but adult Piwi depletion or nuclear localization mutants show largely unchanged H3K9me3 levels, indicating a developmental stage-specific role.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 are supported by differential effects of embryonic versus adult Piwi perturbation on H3K9me3 levels. The distinction between establishment and maintenance is consistent with published findings for piRNA clusters (C81-C82) and extends this model to satDNAs. Some variation among datasets is noted (C83) but the overall pattern is clear.

results.result: SatDNAs are regulated by piRNAs originating from their own genomic loci through a self-regulatory mechanism. Complex satDNA transcription is regulated similarly to dual-strand piRNA clusters, and Piwi, guided by satDNA-derived piRNAs, establishes H3K9me3 at satDNA loci, marking them as piRNA production sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C85, C88, C94, C104 synthesize the major findings into a coherent model. The self-regulation model (C94) is well-supported by the data showing satDNAs produce piRNAs that affect heterochromatin at the same loci. However, C94 is explicitly described as a 'proposed model' and represents an inference from the data rather than direct demonstration of the mechanism.

results.result: The distribution of piRNA reads is non-uniform along satDNA repeat units and differs between ovaries and testes, while Rhino ChIP-seq reads show uniform distribution similar to genomic repeat alignment depth.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53, C60 describe patterns in read distribution supported by computational analysis of sequencing data. The non-uniform piRNA distribution (C52-C53) contrasts with uniform Rhino distribution (C60), suggesting differences in processing or transcription between tissues. The interpretation that this reflects tissue-specific differences in machinery (C53) is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: The piRNA pathway is one of several factors important for proper packaging and regulation of repeat-rich genomic regions. Piwi may not be the only factor necessary for heterochromatin establishment, and maintenance of heterochromatin at piRNA clusters and satDNAs is not Piwi-dependent once established.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 provide appropriate caveats and context for the main findings. C95-C96 are supported by citations and data analysis (Supplementary file 10), while C97 represents a reasonable inference from the data that acknowledges the complexity of heterochromatin regulation.

results.result: The piRNA pathway has a general role in remodeling chromatin in the developing embryo, and initial heterochromatin establishment may be important for ensuring genome integrity throughout development and in adult tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C106 represent broader implications of the findings. While C105 is a reasonable inference from the data, C106 is explicitly stated as speculative ('but this remains an open question'). These claims extend beyond what the data directly demonstrate and would require additional experiments to validate.

results.result: Background and context claims establishing the biological importance of satDNAs, piRNA pathways, and heterochromatin regulation based on prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C9-C31, C40, C86-C87, C89-C92, C98-C103 provide essential background context supported by appropriate citations to published literature. These claims establish the foundation for the study but do not represent new findings from this work.
